lesson.title: The Three-Condition Test for Continuity at a Point
lesson.summary: Continuity at a point comes down to exactly three checkable conditions, and seeing a worked example of each one failing on its own is the fastest way to make the definition stick.
lesson.body:
Building directly on continuity-at-a-point, here is the definition stated as a precise, three-part checklist. A function f is continuous at x = a exactly when all three of the following hold. Condition 1: f(a) is defined, meaning a is actually in the domain of f. Condition 2: lim as x approaches a of f(x) exists as a single finite number, meaning the left-hand and right-hand limits both exist and agree, per limit existence. Condition 3: lim as x approaches a of f(x) equals f(a), meaning the value approached and the value landed on are the same number. All three must hold at once; if even one of them fails, f is discontinuous at a.

Worked example where Condition 1 fails: f(x) = (x^2 - 9) / (x - 3). At a = 3, plugging in directly gives 0/0, so f(3) is undefined and Condition 1 fails immediately, with no need to check the other two conditions at all. Recall from limits-from-tables that the limit here does in fact exist and equals 6, since (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) simplifies to x + 3 for every x not equal to 3. That the limit exists does not rescue continuity when the function value itself is simply missing.

Worked example where Condition 2 fails: f(x) = -1 for x less than 0, and f(x) = 1 for x greater than or equal to 0. At a = 0, f(0) = 1 is defined, so Condition 1 is satisfied. But the left-hand limit as x approaches 0 from the left is -1, while the right-hand limit as x approaches 0 from the right is 1. Since these two one-sided limits disagree, lim as x approaches 0 of f(x) does not exist, so Condition 2 fails, and f is discontinuous at x = 0, a jump discontinuity, even though f(0) itself is perfectly well defined.

Worked example where Condition 3 fails: f(x) = x + 1 for every x not equal to 2, and f(2) = 5, a deliberately relocated single point. Condition 1 holds, since f(2) = 5 is defined. Condition 2 holds, since lim as x approaches 2 of f(x) equals 2 + 1 = 3, with both sides approaching the same line x + 1. But Condition 3 fails: the limit (3) does not equal the function value (5). So f is discontinuous at x = 2, a removable discontinuity, meaning it could be fixed with a single edit, by simply redefining f(2) to equal 3 instead of 5.

Worked example where all three conditions hold: f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 7 at a = 3. Condition 1: f(3) = 9 - 12 + 7 = 4, which is defined. Condition 2: since f is a polynomial, lim as x approaches 3 of f(x) equals f(3) by direct substitution, because polynomials are continuous everywhere, as shown in the continuity chapter, so the limit exists and equals 4. Condition 3: the limit (4) equals the function value (4), a match. All three conditions hold, so f is continuous at x = 3, exactly as expected for a polynomial at any point of its domain.

As a practical takeaway, when asked to justify continuity, or the lack of it, at a specific point, work through the three conditions in order and stop as soon as one fails. The condition that fails also identifies the type of discontinuity: a missing function value points to a hole with nothing plotted there, disagreeing one-sided limits point to a jump, and a fine limit that simply does not match a relocated function value points to a removable hole with a stray point elsewhere, tying together every discontinuity type introduced across this whole chapter sequence.
